props.title: Tower of London

sections.content: **Tower of London** (1939) stands as a fascinating early horror-historical hybrid, with Boris Karloff delivering a chilling performance as the executioner Mord. The film reimagines Richard III's bloody rise to power through a Universal Horror lens, complete with atmospheric castle sets and gothic imagery. Director Rowland V. Lee, fresh off **Son of Frankenstein** (1939), brings the same moody aesthetic to this medieval tale. While historically inaccurate, it established a template for combining period drama with horror elements that influenced later films like **The Curse of the Werewolf** (1961) and **Witchfinder General** (1968). Tower of London|1939|Boris Karloff stars in this horror-tinged historical drama about Richard III's murderous path to the throne|Tubi Richard III|1955|Laurence Olivier's definitive Shakespeare adaptation brings the hunchbacked king to vivid life|HBO Max The Private Life of Henry VIII|1933|Charles Laughton's Oscar-winning portrayal of the infamous Tudor monarch|Criterion Channel

The film marked an important shift in how Hollywood approached historical subjects, injecting genre elements to create hybrid entertainment. This approach influenced later medieval-horror crossovers like **Black Sunday** (1960) and **The Masque of the Red Death** (1964). Basil Rathbone's portrayal of Richard III predates Olivier's famous interpretation and offers a more overtly villainous take that aligns with horror conventions rather than Shakespearean tradition. SUBHEAD: Gothic Horror Meets Historical Drama

The production design by Jack Otterson deserves special attention for creating a properly menacing Tower of London that rivals Universal's classic horror castles. These sets would influence countless later medieval horror films, from Roger Corman's Poe cycle to **The Conqueror Worm** (1968). The film's success also paved the way for other historical figures to receive the horror treatment, notably in films like **Burke & Hare** (1971) and the later remake **Tower of London** (1962) with Vincent Price.
